idiom_name: ActiveRecord model class + relation objects (where/scopes) as the collection surface
implementation_notes: In Rails the repository is already there: the model class stands for the collection and Invoice.where(due: ...on) returns a lazily evaluated ActiveRecord::Relation that chains (order, limit, includes), while named scopes give it domain language and save/destroy are the collection operations - a repository class would duplicate this. What a repository still buys is persistence ignorance: when the domain must not inherit from ActiveRecord::Base, write a plain-Ruby repository that talks to the model class internally and returns POROs, keeping every relation call inside the repository (never returning a Relation, which would hand query building back to the caller). That classic form is justified when the domain model is meant to be framework-free or when the same interface needs an in-memory double.
pitfalls: A Relation is lazy and re-evaluable: returning it from the repository leaks query building to callers and lets later chaining change the result set - call to_a/load at the boundary.
A Relation carries the ActiveRecord class and connection, so an in-memory fake cannot return one without the ORM; design the interface around plain Ruby objects if you need doubles.
default_scope and association conditions silently restrict relations, so a repository method built on a default-scoped model returns fewer rows than its name promises.
